subject: Cooking
title: Bubble Tea: Taiwan's Global Export
description: A micro-lesson that makes Bubble Tea: Taiwan's Global Export usable.

hook.text: Chewy tapioca balls in sweet milk tea — bubble tea went from a Taiwanese night market drink to a $4.3 billion industry.

buildup.text: Invented in Taichung in the 1980s, two tea shops (Chun Shui Tang and Hanlin) both claim credit. The debate rages.

discovery.text: Tapioca pearls are made from cassava starch — cooked until chewy, then soaked in sugar syrup for sweetness.

twist.text: A single bubble tea can contain 500+ calories and 50g of sugar — more than a can of soda.

climax.text: Bubble tea chains like Gong Cha and Tiger Sugar have thousands of locations across Asia, Europe, and the Americas.

punchline.text: Two tea shops argued over who invented it. The world drank 4 billion cups and moved on.

details.summary: Bubble tea originated in Taiwan in the 1980s when tapioca pearls were added to sweetened milk tea, creating a chewy, sippable drink that became a global youth phenomenon. The tapioca pearls called boba must be cooked fresh daily for proper texture.
details.whyItMatters: Bubble tea is one of the most successful food innovations of the last 40 years. Its spread from Taiwanese night markets to worldwide chain stores demonstrates how novel texture drives food trends.
takeaways: Invented in Taiwan in the 1980s by adding tapioca to milk tea
Tapioca pearls must be cooked fresh daily for optimal chewy texture
Global bubble tea revenue exceeds $4 billion annually

faq.question: Why did bubble tea become so popular globally?
faq.answer: The combination of sweet, creamy tea with chewy tapioca pearls created a completely novel texture experience. Instagram-friendly aesthetics amplified its spread. Customization options — sugar levels, ice levels, toppings — appeal to personalization culture.

faq.question: What are boba pearls made from?
faq.answer: Traditional boba pearls are made from tapioca starch extracted from cassava root, mixed with water and brown sugar for color. They are rolled into balls and boiled until chewy. The pearls must be used within hours — they harden when cold.
